We show that monoculture is inherently subjective, relying on two key decisions: 1) the baseline null model for what "independence" should look like; and 2) the population of models and items under consideration. We conclude with concrete guidelines for future evaluators to ensure the robustness of their results.

items.title: Adaptive Estimation and Inference in Conditional Moment Models via the Discrepancy Principle
items.description: arXiv:2603.01337v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study adaptive estimation and inference in linear inverse problems defined by conditional moment restrictions. These problems are typically ill-posed, so estimators require regularization, yet the optimal regularization strength depends on a source parameter that is almost never known. We develop a discrepancy principle that chooses this parameter from empirical losses and prescribed bounds on statistical error, without knowing the source parameter. The framework covers Regularized DeepIV (RDIV) and the Tikhonov Regularized Adversarial Estimator (TRAE). Under the stated realizability conditions and comparable fitting and calibration error bounds, both one-step procedures attain strong- and weak-error bounds that match known-source rates for source parameters up to one. We also extend the framework to iterative procedures under realizability of the population iterates, widening the range of source parameters covered by the rate comparison. Finally, we use these adaptive estimators to construct an asymptotically normal doubly robust estimator that adapts to the well-posedness of the primal and dual problems.

items.title: Catalogue-Grounded Multimodal Attribution for Museum Video under Resource and Regulatory Constraints
items.description: arXiv:2603.11147v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Museum audiovisual archives are important records of visual culture, yet in-gallery video remains difficult to search because it lacks catalogue-compatible metadata. We propose CaGMulA, catalogue-grounded multimodal attribution for museum video: a locally deployable pipeline that combines video-language models, structured catalogue retrieval, and abstention-aware decision policies. The system summarises visible artworks, generates catalogue-style descriptions, and attributes title and artist only when evidence is sufficient. We evaluate VideoLLaMA2 and Qwen2-VL across four model configurations and four attribution modes on 18 in-gallery videos. Open-ended generation fails under conservative conditions, producing 0\% coverage across models. By contrast, closed-set catalogue retrieval reaches 100\% coverage with 62\% accepted title--artist correctness, while a verifier-gated hybrid mode reduces coverage to 50\% but improves accepted correctness to 78\%. The results show that reliable museum-video attribution is driven less by unrestricted generation than by catalogue grounding, visual retrieval, and selective abstention for curatorial review.

items.title: Multi-Domain Empirical Bayes for Linearly-Mixed Causal Representations
items.description: arXiv:2603.18404v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to learn low-dimensional causal latent variables from high-dimensional observations. While identifiability has been extensively studied for CRL, estimation has been less explored. We use empirical Bayes (EB) to estimate causal representations from multiple domains whose differences reflect interventions in a shared causal model. Multi-domain CRL poses a simultaneous inference problem suited to EB. Here, we propose an EB $f$-modeling algorithm that improves the quality of learned causal variables by exploiting invariant structure within and across domains. Specifically, we consider linear measurement models with interventional priors induced by an acyclic latent causal model with known graph and intervention targets. We develop an EM-style algorithm based on causally structured score matching. In experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic single-cell data, our proposed method achieves more accurate estimation than alternative methods and baselines.

items.title: Formulation and Learning Of The Forecasting Problem
items.description: arXiv:2603.20359v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning has opened new frontiers in purely data-driven forecasting of dynamical systems; the resulting methods are showing considerable promise in some application domains. However, in contrast to model-driven algorithms, analysis of these data-driven methods is poorly developed. In this paper we address this issue, developing a theory to underpin data-driven methods to solve forecasting problems. The theoretical framework comprises two key components: (i) establishing the existence of a mapping defining the forecasting problem; (ii) showing that it is possible to approximate this mapping by supervised learning techniques, to arbitrary accuracy. We work in the continuous-time and noise-free setting as this defines a simple canonical setting in which to establish an underpinning theory; the continuous-time setting leads to an operator formulation of the problem in which the underlying forecasting map is defined on pathspace. As a byproduct of our framework we show that analogous existence and approximation results may be obtained for the smoothing problem of recovering unobserved components of dynamical systems, from observed components, using supervised learning. The theoretical results, for both forecasting and smoothing, are illustrated with experiments studying the Lorenz `63, Lorenz `96 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamical systems.

items.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Medical Image Representation Learning
items.description: arXiv:2603.23794v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision foundation models (FMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance in medical imaging. However, they encode information in abstract latent representations that clinicians cannot interrogate or verify. The goal of this study is to investigate Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for replacing opaque FM image representations with human-interpretable, sparse features. We train SAEs on embeddings from BiomedParse (biomedical) and DINOv3 (general-purpose) using 909,873 CT and MRI 2D image slices from the TotalSegmentator dataset. We find that learned sparse features: (a) reconstruct original embeddings with high fidelity (R2 up to 0.941) and recover up to 87.8% of downstream performance using only 10 features (99.4% dimensionality reduction), (b) preserve semantic fidelity in image retrieval tasks, (c) correspond to specific concepts that can be expressed in language using large language model (LLM)-based auto-interpretation. (d) bridge clinical language and abstract latent representations in zero-shot language-driven image retrieval. Our work indicates SAEs are a promising pathway towards interpretable, concept-driven medical vision systems. Code repository: https://github.com/pwesp/sail.

items.title: Minimaxity and Admissibility of Bayesian Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2604.04673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) offer a natural probabilistic formulation for inference in deep learning models. Despite their popularity, their optimality has received limited attention through the lens of statistical decision theory. In this paper, we study decision rules induced by deep, fully connected feedforward ReLU BNNs in the normal location model under quadratic loss. We show that, for fixed prior scales, the induced Bayes decision rule is not minimax. We then propose a hyperprior on the effective output variance of the BNN prior that yields a superharmonic square-root marginal density, establishing that the resulting decision rule is simultaneously admissible and minimax. We further extend these results from the quadratic loss setting to the predictive density estimation problem with Kullback--Leibler loss. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings numerically through simulation.

items.title: A Continuous-Time Actor-Critic Framework for Jump-Diffusion Controls with Normalizing Flows
items.description: arXiv:2604.05398v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continuous-time stochastic control with time-inhomogeneous jump-diffusion dynamics is central in finance and economics, but computing optimal policies is difficult under explicit time dependence, discontinuous shocks, and high dimensionality. We propose an actor-critic framework that serves as a mesh-free solver for entropy-regularized control problems and stochastic games with jumps. The approach is built on a time-inhomogeneous little q-function and an appropriate occupation measure, yielding a policy-gradient representation that accommodates time-dependent drift, volatility, and jump terms. To represent expressive stochastic policies in continuous-action spaces, we parameterize the actor using conditional normalizing flows, enabling flexible non-Gaussian policies while retaining exact likelihood evaluation for entropy regularization and policy optimization. We validate the method on time-inhomogeneous linear-quadratic control, Merton portfolio optimization, and a multi-agent portfolio game, using explicit solutions or high-accuracy benchmarks. Numerical results demonstrate stable learning under jump discontinuities, accurate approximation of optimal stochastic policies, and favorable scaling with respect to dimension and number of agents.

items.title: Iterative Identification Closure: Amplifying Causal Identifiability in Linear SEMs
items.description: arXiv:2604.09309v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Half-Trek Criterion (HTC) is the primary graphical tool for determining generic identifiability of causal effect coefficients in linear structural equation models (SEMs) with latent confounders. However, HTC is inherently node-wise: it simultaneously resolves all incoming edges of a node, leaving a gap of "inconclusive" causal effects (15-23% in moderate graphs). We introduce Iterative Identification Closure (IIC), a general framework that decouples causal identification into two phases: (1) a seed function S_0 that identifies an initial set of edges from any external source of information (instrumental variables, interventions, non-Gaussianity, prior knowledge, etc.); and (2) Reduced HTC propagation that iteratively substitutes known coefficients to reduce system dimension, enabling identification of edges that standard HTC cannot resolve. The core novelty is iterative identification propagation: newly identified edges feed back to unlock further identification -- a mechanism absent from all existing graphical criteria, which treat each edge (or node) in isolation. This propagation is non-trivial: coefficient substitution alters the covariance structure, and soundness requires proving that the modified Jacobian retains generic full rank -- a new theoretical result (Reduced HTC Theorem). We prove that IIC is sound, monotone, converges in O(|E|) iterations (empirically <=2), and strictly subsumes both HTC and ancestor decomposition. Exhaustive verification on all graphs with n<=5 (134,144 edges) confirms 100% precision (zero false positives); with combined seeds, IIC reduces the HTC gap by over 80%. The propagation gain is gamma~4x (2 seeds identifying ~3% of edges to 97.5% total identification), far exceeding gamma<=1.2x of prior methods that incorporate side information without iterative feedback.

items.title: Gradient Descent's Last Iterate is Often (slightly) Suboptimal
items.description: arXiv:2604.13870v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the well-studied setting of minimizing a convex Lipschitz function using either gradient descent (GD) or its stochastic variant (SGD), and examine the last iterate convergence. We prove that $\Theta(\sqrt{\log(T)/T})$ is the optimal anytime rate attainable with a fixed stepsize schedule (that does not depend on the total number of steps $T$). The upper bound holds already for SGD, and improves on the $\log(T)/\sqrt{T}$ rate of Shamir and Zhang [2013], as well as the $\sqrt{\log(T)/T}$ rate of Zamani and Glineur [2023] which was proven only for deterministic GD. The matching lower bound holds already for GD, and confirms the conjecture of Jain et al. [2019], namely that the optimal $1/\sqrt{T}$ rate for the last iterate cannot be obtained without prior knowledge of $T$.

items.title: CrystalREPA: Transferring Physical Priors from Universal MLIPs to Crystal Generative Models
items.description: arXiv:2605.08960v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Crystal generative models mainly learn what stable crystals look like, with little explicit supervision for what makes them stable. We reveal a substantial representation gap between state-of-the-art crystal generative models and pretrained universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) via energy probing, and show this gap can be closed by a simple training-time alignment. We propose Crystal REPresentation Alignment (CrystalREPA), a plug-and-play framework that aligns the atom-wise hidden states of generative encoders with frozen MLIP representations through an element-aware contrastive objective, transferring stability-aware atomistic priors with marginal training overhead and no additional inference cost. Across three generative frameworks, ten MLIP teachers, and two benchmark datasets, CrystalREPA consistently improves the thermodynamic stability, structural validity, and structural fidelity of generated crystals. Equally important, we find that an MLIP's transfer effectiveness is poorly predicted by its accuracy on standard leaderboards (e.g., Matbench Discovery) but strongly predicted by the distinguishability of its atom-wise representation space, yielding a practical, accuracy-independent criterion for selecting MLIP teachers for generative transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/Chengqian-Zhang/CrystalREPA.

items.title: Unified Approach for Weakly Supervised Multicalibration
items.description: arXiv:2605.09857v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multicalibration requires predicted scores to agree with label probabilities across rich families of subgroups and score-dependent tests, but existing methods require clean input-label pairs for evaluation and post-processing. This assumption fails in weakly supervised learning (WSL) regimes -- including positive-unlabeled, unlabeled-unlabeled, and positive-confidence learning -- where clean labels are costly or unavailable even though reliable uncertainty estimates may be crucial. We address this gap by developing estimators of multicalibration error and post-hoc correction methods for WSL settings in which clean input-label pairs are unavailable. We propose a unified framework for estimating and correcting multicalibration under weak supervision by combining contamination-matrix risk rewrites with witness-based calibration constraints, yielding corrected multicalibration moments with finite-sample guarantees. We further propose weak-label multicalibration boost (WLMC), a generic post-hoc recalibration algorithm under weak supervision. Finally, we conduct experiments across multiple weak-supervision settings to evaluate multicalibration behavior and offer empirical insight into uncertainty estimation under weak supervision.

items.title: Stay Fair! Ensuring Group Fairness in Diffusion Models Across Guidance Scales
items.description: arXiv:2605.28036v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models steer conditional generation with a tunable guidance scale to trade off prompt alignment and diversity. However, existing debiasing techniques are optimized for a single scale, degrading fairness when users adjust this parameter. We trace this behavior to a previously overlooked source by decomposing total bias into two components: a model bias and a guidance bias. While prior work primarily targets the former, we show that the guidance bias varies with the guidance scale, persisting even in models that have already been debiased. To address this, we extend Strong Demographic Parity to guidance and derive a condition under which the target distribution retains its group ratio across guidance scales. Building on this condition, we propose StayFair, which designs fair guidance algorithms in both regimes. For classifier guidance, it equalizes the classifier's output distributions across groups; for classifier-free guidance, it shifts the null embedding by a prompt-dependent offset. Because StayFair modifies only the guidance step, it is orthogonal to model debiasing and can be layered onto existing fair diffusion models. Across class-conditional and text-to-image generation, StayFair decouples fairness from the guidance scale without sacrificing image quality. Our decomposition also enables a more detailed analysis of the sources of bias in diffusion models.

items.title: FlatVPR: Plug-and-play Geo-linear Residual Adapter for Geometric Rectification of Foundation Model Feature Manifolds
items.description: arXiv:2606.01734v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper proposes ``FlatVPR,'' a novel geometric rectification paradigm that effectively bridges the trade-off between map lightweightness and localization accuracy in visual place recognition (VPR) by enforcing a feature manifold structure where any descriptor between two adjacent anchors $\mathbf{z}_A$ and $\mathbf{z}_B$ can be accurately reconstructed via linear interpolation $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{pseudo} = (1-t)\mathbf{z}_A + t\mathbf{z}_B$, where $t \in [0,1]$ denotes the relative position. While state-of-the-art foundation models such as DINOv2-ViT-S/14 provide robust semantic features, their latent manifolds exhibit prominent curvature, projecting uniform linear motion in physical space onto highly non-linear trajectories in the feature space, which hinders reliable reconstruction under sparse anchor conditions. To enable the aforementioned interpolation-based reconstruction, we introduce a residual transformation $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{z} + \text{Res}(\mathbf{z})$ to the raw foundation features $\mathbf{z}$, where $\text{Res}(\cdot)$ represents a learnable adapter. Our method explicitly suppresses manifold curvature using a mathematically grounded Pullback Flatness Loss that minimizes the deviation of intermediate features from the linear segment connecting adjacent anchors, thereby minimizing the intrinsic curvature of the manifold. Through this spatial flattening, map construction is formulated within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework, decoupled into a continuous M-step for manifold adaptation and a conceptual E-step for optimal anchor selection guidelines. Experiments on the NCLT dataset demonstrate that the application of our adapter leads to significant performance improvements even under extremely sparse anchor conditions with 100m intervals and extreme seasonal changes.

items.title: Learning Action-Conditional and Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting World Models for Rigid Objects
items.description: arXiv:2606.01950v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: World models enable intelligent agents to predict the consequences of their actions on the environment. In this paper, we propose Multi Rigid Object Gaussian World Model (MRO-GWM), a novel model that learns action-conditional dynamics of rigid objects in 3D. Using object-centric Gaussians, we can represent arbitrary object shapes and multi-object scenes. We develop a novel temporal-spatial transformer architecture that predicts future rigid body motion from a history of object Gaussians and future actions. Objects are represented by Gaussians in an object-centric frame, which allows to describe object motion as a rigid body transformation. Our model is trained on reconstructions from multiple viewpoints, which requires the model to also handle partial observations of objects due to occlusions. We analyze prediction performance of our approach on synthetic datasets composed of typical household objects with multi-object dynamics and interactions by a robot end effector. We also evaluate our model in model-predictive control for non-prehensile manipulation in simulation and for image-based tracking and prediction of object motion in simulated and real-world scenes.

items.title: Differentiable FEM versus PINN for pavement layer inverse analysis: enforcing physics as hard or soft constraints
items.description: arXiv:2606.03210v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic-differentiation-based inverse analysis methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and differentiable programming, have recently shown great promise due to their ability to compute accurate gradients and convergence efficiency. However, their applicability to falling weight deflectometer (FWD) backcalculation remains unexplored. This study critically evaluates PINN-based inverse analysis for a multilayer pavement system and investigates differentiable finite element method (DiffFEM) as an alternative based on a synthetic benchmark. The standard PINN does not recover layer moduli because of the sharp domain discontinuities inherent to layered pavement systems. Although we use an extended PINN with domain decomposition (XPINN), which shows better performance on discontinuous domains, its performance remains highly sensitive to loss weighting and network architecture, and degrades under measurement noise. By contrast, DiffFEM consistently achieves more accurate, stable, and computationally efficient inversion results. These results show and quantify the expected advantage of DiffFEM, which enforces the governing physics as a hard constraint in the solver, over PINN-based approaches, where the governing physics is imposed as a soft constraint through the loss function. More broadly, the findings suggest that the choice between PINN- and DiffFEM-based inverse analysis needs careful consideration, with DiffFEM offering practical advantages when an efficient and robust differentiable forward solver is available.

items.title: QPredSGG: Hybrid Quantum Predicate Learning for Long-Tailed Scene Graph Generation
items.description: arXiv:2606.04689v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scene Graph Generation (SGG) requires relational reasoning over objects and their interactions, but performance is constrained by long-tail predicate imbalance. Classical SGG models rely on dataset statistics, leading to biased predictions toward frequent relations rather than fine-grained semantic predicates. Although debiasing improves mean recall, predicate classification in existing frameworks still relies on high-dimensional classical decision modules with high parameter overhead. This work introduces a resource-efficient hybrid quantum predicate classifier for SGG by replacing the classical predicate head in the CFEN with a QP-Head trained using class-balanced WCE. To the best of our knowledge, this work is among the first evaluations of a hybrid quantum architecture for scene graph predicate classification on Visual Genome 150. We evaluate the impact of qubit count, encoding strategy, entangling topology, and circuit depth. Under a 4-qubit configuration using Amplitude Embedding and Strongly Entangling Layers, the QP-Head projects 4096-dimensional pair features into a 16-dimensional quantum input while using 96 trainable quantum parameters. Operating within this compressed representation space under WCE training, it achieves strong long-tail recognition, reaching a peak mR@100 of 57.25% compared to the 41.1% mR@100 reported in the CFEN baseline under standard training. Protocol-matched ablations indicate that the primary advantage of the quantum head lies in extreme representational compactness rather than an accuracy gain over full-dimensional weighted classical heads: it achieves global recall within 0.19pp of the 2048-dimensional WCE classical baseline while operating from a 128x smaller head feature space. Scaling to 8 qubits maintains robust long-tail performance (55.38% mR@100 with 384 quantum parameters), while depth analysis highlights expressibility-latency trade-offs.

items.title: MS-COOT: Comparing Morse-Smale Complexes with Co-Optimal Transport
items.description: arXiv:2606.08258v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding and comparing structures in scalar fields is a central challenge in scientific visualization, with applications ranging from feature analysis to temporal and structural comparison. The Morse-Smale (MS) complex provides a natural representation by decomposing a scalar field into regions induced by gradient flow. However, existing approaches typically rely on graph-based representations, matching critical points without explicitly establishing correspondences between regions. In this work, we represent the MS complex as a hypergraph, where critical points form nodes and regions define hyperedges. We introduce MS-COOT, a co-optimal transport distance that jointly computes correspondences between critical points and regions. This formulation enables explicit region-to-region matching within a distance-based framework, allowing identification of region-level events such as splitting and merging. We instantiate this framework with domain-specific components, including a hypernetwork function encoding relationships between critical points and regions, persistence-based probability measures, and a sample cost term that incorporates critical point attributes. We evaluate MS-COOT on datasets spanning 2D simulations, 3D surface meshes, and volumetric data. Our results show that MS-COOT provides distinct characterization of certain region-level structural changes compared to graph-based distances, achieves competitive accuracy in shape classification, and improves classification of simulation parameter settings in a 3D ensemble.

items.title: Minimax PAC Bounds for Learning in Exogenous Contextual MDPs
items.description: arXiv:2606.25170v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a PAC framework in which the learner can access sampling oracles both before and at decision time. Sample complexity is measured by a pair $(n,m)$, where $n$ is the learning budget spent before a query is known and $m$ is the additional sampling budget per query. We demonstrate its relevance in discounted Markov decision processes with exogenous i.i.d.\ contexts revealed before acting. Contexts may affect both rewards and transitions but remain uncontrolled by the agent. The learner can sample the unknown context distribution and the transition kernel. We study policy evaluation (PE), best-value estimation (BVE), and best-policy extraction (BPE). When rewards and transitions are known, a variance-reduced algorithm solves all three tasks with sample complexity $\bigl(\widetilde O((1-\gamma)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2}),0\bigr)$, which is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be the controlled state space. When transitions are also unknown, we give a PE algorithm with complexity $\bigl(\widetilde O(|\mathcal X|(1-\gamma)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2}), \widetilde O((1-\gamma)^{-2}\varepsilon^{-2})\bigr)$ and matching lower bounds at this budget pair. For BVE and BPE, we give an algorithm with a common offline budget $\widetilde O(|\mathcal X|^2|\mathcal A|(1-\gamma)^{-4}\varepsilon^{-2})$ and respective query costs $\widetilde O(|\mathcal A|(1-\gamma)^{-2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ and $\widetilde O(|\mathcal A|(1-\gamma)^{-3}\varepsilon^{-2})$. Importantly, all bounds are independent of the context-space cardinality.

items.title: Determinantal sampling on general spaces: fast approximation via diffusion geometry
items.description: arXiv:2607.06644v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) have recently emerged as a kernel-based alternative to standard independent sampling for constructing efficient minibatches, coresets, and other compact representations of large-scale datasets. One of the key strengths of DPP based samplers is that they can be deployed over very general spaces, in contrast to more classical sampling methods beyond i.i.d. which tend to be tailored to particular well-structured settings, principally Euclidean spaces. In this work, we establish explicit rate guarantees for determinantal sampling in spaces that extend far beyond known Euclidean setups, focussing on spectral kernels obtained from eigenspaces of naturally associated Markov diffusion operators, including in particular the Laplacian on manifolds and nearest-neighbour type graphs on data point clouds and the discrete Schrodinger operator on large scale networks. This covers, in particular, the settings of Riemannian manifolds and discrete networks, as well as the problem of batch sampling from discrete datasets. Overall, our approach achieves guarantees comparable to $\big(\text{sample size}\big)^{-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2d_{\text{int}}}}$ , which match with the rates for well-known determinantal samplers on Euclidean spaces of comparable dimension. In terms of techniques, we connect to the celebrated Weyl's Law for spectra on general spaces, and leverage tools from the theory of Markov diffusion operators and Dirichlet forms, which could be of independent interest in this area. Our approach is applicable to a very wide plethora of ambient spaces beyond Euclidean as soon as these ingredients are available, including e.g. fractals, leading to guarantees that will be governed by the intrinsic structural constants of such spaces.

items.title: Full-data accuracy with fewer labels for training and fine-tuning machine-learning force fields
items.description: arXiv:2607.14486v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) are reliable only near their training distribution, making efficient construction of diverse training sets a major bottleneck for both train-from-scratch and foundation fine-tuning workflows. Active learning can reduce this cost, but standard model-committee uncertainty is impractical for foundation MLFFs because each committee member requires a separate fine-tuning run. We present an active-learning workflow based on last-layer-projection regression (LLPR), a forward-pass-cheap per-configuration uncertainty estimator. Across molecular, condensed-phase, and electrolyte systems, LLPR identifies compact, high-value training sets that recover full-data accuracy using only a small fraction of electronic-structure labels. In foundation-model fine-tuning, LLPR-selected configurations approach the practical fine-tuning ceiling with substantially fewer labels than random selection. In iterative electrolyte fine-tuning, LLPR detects unphysical local coordination before new labelling, calibrates uncertainty in force-error units, and supports retrospective convergence monitoring. The resulting models reproduce reference density and Li--O coordination structure, providing a scalable uncertainty-quantification strategy across MLFF training regimes.

items.title: Isotonic Conformal Inference
items.description: arXiv:2607.16675v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A predictor with small overall bias can still exhibit systematic bias conditional on its predicted value, limiting its reliability for downstream uncertainty quantification and candidate screening. We propose Isotonic Conformal Inference, a unified framework for prediction and multiple testing that separates calibration from inference and exploits the level set structure of an isotonic predictor. This structure enables the computation of localized conformal quantiles and $p$-values while avoiding repeated isotonic refitting across candidate responses. For prediction, we introduce Split Isotonic Conformal Prediction (sICP) and Transductive Isotonic Conformal Prediction (tICP), establish prediction-conditional coverage guarantees for both methods, and characterize their finite-sample and asymptotic self-calibration properties. For selection, we introduce Isotonic Conformal Selection (ICS), which provides finite-sample stratum-conditional false discovery rate control. Experiments on simulated regression problems, a healthcare-utilization dataset, and a high-throughput ADMET drug discovery dataset demonstrate the practical performance of the framework and substantially lower computational costs relative to full transductive baselines.

items.title: Local Search with Correlated Randomness
items.description: arXiv:2607.17469v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The running-time distribution of a randomized algorithm is computed under independent randomness, but independence is rarely what a source guarantees. We study sources $\nu$ satisfying $\nu[w]\le DP[w]^s$ for every finite prefix $w$ of the random tape, where $P$ is an independent reference law, $0<s\le1$, and $D\ge1$; individual choices may be predictable, even determined by the past. The worst-case probability of any closed tape event $E$ is exactly $\min\{1,DC_s(E)\}$, where $C_s(E)$ is the infimum cost of covering $E$ by prefixes of varying depth, a tree max-flow/min-cut identity that makes worst-case survival probabilities exact and optimizable over the algorithm's choices. Three applications follow. For $n$ tasks on one machine, each retried until the next random symbol lies in its success set, every schedule has the same makespan distribution under independent randomness, yet under our constraint two fixed orders miss a linear deadline with worst-case probabilities $1$ and $\exp[-\Theta(n)]$; a static priority rule is optimal at every deadline. For the standard local walk on a $k$-CNF with an assignment that satisfies a majority of each clause, we determine the sharp source threshold $s_*$. Below $s_*$, on some instances a single admissible source forces nontermination however clauses are selected; at $s_*$, with fixed $D$, the expected number of flips is at most cubic in the initial Hamming distance, against linear under independence, with matching worst-case instances; and any fixed margin above $s_*$ restores linear dependence on the distance. Third, verified backtracking for noisy predecessor search remains correct under a sufficiently strong bound on the comparison errors. In every setting the algorithm may also restart, which supplies no fresh randomness; restarting restores exponential tails exactly when the nontermination event has a prefix cover of cost below one.

items.title: Label-Free Finite-Volume-Residual Training of Attention Graph Neural Networks for Coupled Thermo-Fluid Fields
items.description: arXiv:2607.20321v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural surrogates are widely used in scientific machine learning for fast prediction of three-dimensional (3D) thermo-fluid fields. However, generating training data using conventional numerical solvers often incurs substantial computational and storage costs. We propose to train an attention graph neural network by minimizing the finite-volume method (FVM) residuals of the governing equations. These residuals are evaluated directly on the mesh, requiring no labeled data. We evaluate the trained surrogates against computational fluid dynamics (CFD) references and a data-supervised baseline across four scenarios. On the two steady-state benchmarks, each solved on the same mesh as its CFD reference, the FVM-loss model reproduces the reference flow and temperature fields with mean field-averaged normalized root-mean-square errors (nRMSEs) near 3%, including the buoyancy-energy coupling. On the two parametric transient cases, the FVM-loss model attains lower rollout errors than the supervised baseline in almost every field, while avoiding the data-generation cost entirely. These results indicate that the FVM loss can provide a practical training signal for neural surrogates and reduce the model development cost.

items.title: Staged Multi-Agent Training for Human-Exoskeleton Co-Adaptation: Simulation-Based Learning and Real-World Metabolic and Biomechanical Validation
items.description: arXiv:2608.00715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning-based controllers can enable exoskeleton assistance to be trained entirely in physics-based simulation, but achieving effective assistance on real users remains challenging because the human and device continuously adapt to one another. We investigate a Staged Multi-Agent Training (SMAT) approach that jointly trains a musculoskeletal human actor and a bilateral hip-exoskeleton actor (control policy) to learn coordinated assistance strategies while accounting for human-device co-adaptation. The resulting policy was transferred to a physical hip exoskeleton and evaluated in eight healthy adults across users and locomotion conditions without subject-specific retraining. Indirect calorimetry was used to compare no-exoskeleton, passive, and active conditions. Active assistance reduced net metabolic rate by 19.7% relative to the passive device (p < 0.001). The policy produced predominantly positive hip mechanical power across subjects, with a positive-power ratio of 0.984, and maintained effective assistance across walking speeds and terrains beyond the training conditions. These results demonstrate that simulation-based multi-agent co-adaptation can produce a single transferable exoskeleton policy that elicits meaningful physiological benefits in real users without subject-specific retraining, providing a framework for reducing the experimental burden of human-in-the-loop controller development.

items.title: Parity-equivariant prediction of conformer-resolved electronic circular dichroism spectra accelerates absolute configuration assignment
items.description: arXiv:2608.21892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electronic circular dichroism (ECD) is a key experimental probe for assigning the absolute configuration of chiral molecules, but interpreting measured spectra often requires costly time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. The few existing machine learning methods for ECD prediction are faster, but their accuracy still falls well short of that required for experimental applications. Here we introduce PhysECD, a parity-aware E(3)-equivariant framework that builds the spectrum from its underlying quantum-chemical quantities, ensuring correct chiroptical symmetry by construction. To improve generalization and support experimental applications, we construct SCECD, a conformer-resolved dataset of 578,104 computed spectra spanning diverse natural products with one to five stereocentres. PhysECD predicts ECD spectra from conformer geometries in milliseconds, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the CMCDS benchmark and SCECD. Validation against 77 experimental spectra further demonstrates that PhysECD can serve as a fast alternative to TDDFT for assigning the absolute configuration of complex chiral molecules.

items.title: Explainable GeoAI for urban wildfire structure loss: vegetation and built environment in the 2025 Palisades Fire
items.description: arXiv:2608.22293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Urban wildfire resilience depends on interactions among built form, vegetation condition, and extreme fire weather, yet city-scale risk models often overlook whether predictive skill transfers across neighborhoods. We developed a spatially validated GeoAI workflow for the January 2025 Palisades Fire, linking 12,081 CAL FIRE damage inspections to pre-fire Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, Landsat surface temperature, LANDFIRE fuels, terrain, and OpenStreetMap buildings and roads. Among 9,883 inspected residential structures, 5,566 were destroyed. Random cross-validation yielded ROC-AUC 0.92 for the integrated XGBoost model, but 1 km spatial block validation reduced performance to 0.75; logistic regression performed similarly and was better calibrated. Building count within 100 m was the strongest predictor, with destruction odds increasing 4.12-fold per standard deviation. Vegetation moisture and greenness showed opposing conditional associations: NDMI at 100-300 m was protective (OR 0.52), whereas NDVI at 30-100 m was positively associated with destruction after accounting for moisture (OR 1.74). Predictive information was concentrated at the 100-300 m neighborhood scale. A separate post-fire track mapped burn severity and vegetation recovery without leakage. The results support neighborhood-scale susceptibility screening, moisture-aware vegetation management, and spatial block validation as a minimum standard for single-event urban wildfire modeling.

items.title: Mirror descent algorithms with logarithmic barriers
items.description: arXiv:2608.22834v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We derive convergence guarantees for mirror descent and proximal mirror descent with a logarithmic barrier as the distance-generating function. When the solution lies on the boundary, the Bregman divergence blows up and classical guarantees become vacuous. While existing remedies recover $O(\log k/k)$ rates by adapting classical bounds, we propose a more direct route in which the Bregman distance to the solution never appears, and which achieves the same rate with constant stepsize. We also construct an example showing that this rate cannot be improved in general. Finally, we compare the proposed approach with interior-point methods.

items.title: WAVE: Wavelet-Controlled Coarse-to-Fine Guidance for Depth Super-Resolution
items.description: arXiv:2608.25302v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Guided depth super-resolution (GDSR) typically extracts RGB guidance features through convolutional hierarchies, inheriting their fine-to-coarse bias. Thus, low-level spatial cues surface in early layers, leaving the deeper layers to suppress those that do not correspond to true depth boundaries, which risks artifacts and blurred edges. The same fine-to-coarse bias persists in semantics-based methods that consume low-level tokens early and global tokens late. We present WAVE, which introduces a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (ML-DWT) as an explicit and interpretable feature-control mechanism, enabling a coarse-to-fine reconstruction by consuming sub-bands and semantic tokens in reverse of their generation order. WAVE further exploits these sub-bands to treat high- and low-frequency content separately, isolating the misleading RGB color and texture cues before any feature is learned so that their admission can be controlled explicitly, offering an intuitive alternative to the suppression learned implicitly by an opaque network. WAVE separates structure and detail reconstruction into dedicated modules that: i) model interactions within and across wavelet sub-bands, depth features, and semantic priors, ii) apply semantic gating to the high-frequency bands, and iii) fuse modalities through an invertible coupling mechanism that prevents collapse onto a single modality. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that WAVE matches or outperforms existing methods, with the largest gains at high upsampling factors, where low-resolution depth contains the least structure.

items.title: FUSION: a skill-based research agent for publicly obtainable nuclear-physics codes
items.description: arXiv:2609.04742v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Running an unfamiliar nuclear-physics code is rarely difficult because of the physics alone. One must find and build the program, learn its input conventions, and decide whether a plausible output is actually correct. A general-purpose coding agent helps with the first two tasks but may make the last one harder: it can write an input file that runs with the wrong physical convention. FUSION addresses this problem with code-specific skills. A skill obtains the code from its public source, starts from a verified input, runs and parses the calculation, records known failure modes, and must reproduce a stated benchmark to a stated tolerance before reporting a result. The current release covers twenty codes, spanning optical models and reactions, nuclear structure, fission and statistical models, astrophysics and R-matrix analysis, and heavy-ion transport. It also includes an offline, searchable collection of 61 167 pages derived from the nucl-th literature. User notes and credentials remain outside the public repository. FUSION is available under the MIT license at https://github.com/jinleiphys/FUSION; documentation is at https://vibeinscience.com. Here I describe the design, the checks behind the current release, and one complete calculation from input to comparison with measured data.

items.title: Broken on Arrival: Non-Functional Quantized LLM Artifacts in Public Model Registries and How to Catch Them
items.description: arXiv:2609.05881v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Developers download quantized large language models (LLMs) from public registries to run them locally. None of the registries we examined documented functional testing of their files. We tested all 305 eligible code-capable GGUF tags (the llama.cpp format) across 15 model lines in the official Ollama library, plus 22 popular Hugging Face community files. A 15-task code screen identified suspects, which we retested on all 164 HumanEval+ tasks. Seven official tags (2.3%) solved at most six of them. All were low-bit quantizations of models with at most four billion parameters. We rebuilt five suspect files from the original weights. All five registry files matched our uncalibrated rebuilds tensor for tensor, so none was corrupted. Exact reproducibility did not imply function. With the weights, toolchain and tensor mix held fixed, adding an importance matrix raised three Qwen2.5-Coder-3B builds from zero to 76-113 solved tasks. The same uncalibrated recipe left the smaller Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B functional, showing that the recipe alone does not predict failure. None of 66 sampled tags that passed the screen was non-functional. We release the audit data and the quantcheck tool and recommend screening low-bit tags before publication, then calibrating or withholding failures.

items.title: When Can You Trust Your Synthetic Users? Diagnostics and Corrections for LLM Consumer Panels
items.description: arXiv:2609.13148v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate consumers, yet agreement with aggregate survey outcomes can conceal errors in the subgroup estimates that guide decisions. We develop a framework for deciding when to trust, correct, or abandon a synthetic consumer panel by distinguishing population mismatch from differences in conditional responses. The framework combines diagnostics for covariate overlap, conditional calibration, and stability across models with an augmented inverse probability weighting estimator that treats LLM predictions as auxiliary information. Correction requires a complete invitation frame, response indicators for everyone invited, and human outcomes for respondents, together with assumptions of missing at random and positivity. We evaluate the framework using simulations and controlled nonresponse experiments constructed from paired human and LLM responses in ANES and Twin-2K-500. In identified simulation regimes, point bias remains small when either the response model or the outcome model is correct, but nominal 95\% confidence intervals cover only 88--94\% in some regimes. When nonresponse depends on missing human outcomes, substantial bias persists and coverage approaches zero. Controlled masking of the paired datasets reproduces this contrast between successful point correction under imposed missing at random and failure under nonignorable nonresponse. These findings show why validation must address the intended population and task, and why the scope for correcting synthetic estimates depends on the available human data and the assumptions that identify the target.

items.title: A Sentinel-2 benchmark dataset for deep-learning active-fire segmentation across 25 California wildfires, July 2020-August 2026
items.description: arXiv:2609.16199v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This article describes an open image dataset for developing and evaluating active-fire segmentation methods in satellite imagery. The dataset contains 2,148 image-mask pairs from 25 California wildfires, with acquisitions spanning July 2020 to August 2026. Each image is a 512x512-pixel, three-channel composite derived from Sentinel-2 Level-2A bands B12, B11 and B8A at 20 m spatial sampling. A fixed linear rendering is applied throughout the dataset. Corresponding masks distinguish background, SWIR-rule active fire and invalid observations. The masks were generated from shortwave-infrared brightness and near-infrared contrast, followed by constrained neighborhood growth. The release includes chip-level metadata and an incident-disjoint partition containing 18 training, three validation and four test fires. Among the image pairs, 841 contain active-fire labels; these labels occupy 0.0766% of all grid cells. A mask-blind analyst review covers 233 test chips and provides a separate assessment of the rule-generated labels at chip and connected-component levels. Reference training and evaluation code accompanies the data, including a ResNet-34 U-Net implementation with validation-based checkpoint and threshold selection. The archived images, masks, metadata and review annotations support research on rare-class segmentation, learning from algorithmic labels and transfer across fire incidents. The versioned dataset is deposited on Zenodo, with preparation and reuse software maintained in a public GitHub repository.

items.title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
items.description: arXiv:2609.17736v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

items.title: Geometry-Dependent Approximation for Non-Monotone $k$-Submodular Maximization
items.description: arXiv:2610.04049v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the maximization of a nonnegative $k$-submodular function, not assumed monotone, in which each of $n$ elements receives one of $k\ge2$ labels or stays unselected and the selected elements must satisfy a constraint. For a compact convex down-closed region $P\subseteq[0,1]^n$ of fractional selection vectors, the diagonal level $\zeta(P)=\max\{t\in[0,1]:t(1,\ldots,1)\in P\}$ is the largest selection probability that can be given to all elements at once; it equals $r/n$ for a uniform matroid of rank $r$, and $\zeta(P)=1$ means that the constraint is vacuous. We give approximation coefficients that increase continuously with $\zeta$. They come from one inequality for the multilinear extension of the objective: the algorithm computes an action without querying the objective, and objective feedback gives a comparator-independent update direction. For $k\ge3$, feasibility of the action reduces to three polynomial inequalities in one variable; for $k=2$ the profile is closed form. At $\zeta=0$ the coefficients are $0.4456\ldots$ for $k=2$ and $0.4541\ldots$ for every $k\ge3$. For every finite $k\ge3$ they reach $1/2$ above an explicit level, which is $0.4026\ldots$ for $k=3,4,5$, and at $\zeta=1$ they reach $1/2$ for $k=2$, $(\sqrt{17}-3)/2$ for $k=3,4$, and $k/(2k-1)$ for $k\ge5$. Online linear optimization gives $O(\sqrt T)$ approximate regret, with gradient feedback or with value queries made after each action. The coefficients carry over to matroids, with expected and high-probability guarantees, and to any fixed number of knapsacks: the zero-level coefficients hold on every instance, and the larger ones when items are small or when prefix enumeration keeps the diagonal level on one branch. For one budget the enumeration exponent is $O(1/\varepsilon)$.

items.title: Beyond Perturbation Magnitude: Direction-Dependent Responses in Multimodal Geometric Representations
items.description: arXiv:2610.08533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Geometric alignment scores based on Gram determinants provide a compact way to model higher-order consistency among modalities, yet how such scores respond to modality degradation is poorly understood. This paper asks whether the response of a multimodal geometric score is determined primarily by the magnitude of the perturbation-induced displacement. Using frozen cohorts from MSR-VTT (N=878) and DiDeMo (N=980), we apply controlled video blur and audio noise and analyze the response in the relational geometry on which the score is defined. Displacement magnitude explains at most 15% of the out-of-sample variance in the absolute response, and magnitude-matched pairs respond systematically differently, so scalar magnitude does not organize the response. The closed-form first-order expansion of the Gramian volume yields the Directional Geometric Response (DGR): the projection of the displacement onto the local volume gradient, which jointly captures the clean operating point, displacement magnitude, and displacement direction. The absolute first-order DGR term explains the observed response with out-of-sample R^2 of 0.838-0.969, matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963, and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989, whereas the tested direction-free alternatives remain weak or unstable under the corresponding evaluation protocols. A pre-specified gain-normalization candidate, V/(g_V+eps), fails its predictability and clean-order gates. DGR uses the observed degraded-state displacement and is therefore an explanatory quantity, not a deployment-time predictor: geometric response depends on where the representation operates, how far degradation moves the relational geometry, and in which direction it moves.

items.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
items.description: arXiv:2610.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation
items.description: arXiv:2610.19781v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables language models to generate graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints, such as chemical valence and ordering rules, thereby guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences while sticking to standard language modeling for effective training. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.

items.title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
items.description: arXiv:2610.21433v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.

items.title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
items.description: arXiv:2610.26833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

items.title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2610.27606v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $\epsilon$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

items.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
items.description: arXiv:2610.29111v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting molecular magnetic properties often requires costly electronic-structure calculations that account for spin-orbit coupling. Inspired by the spinor nature of the underlying electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features alongside the integer-rank tensors used in conventional equivariant models. We initialize spinors from eigenvectors of an approximate Hamiltonian that includes spin-orbit coupling. The network preserves their rotation laws and makes predictions independent of arbitrary eigenbasis choices. Comparisons with geometry-only and Hamiltonian-informed baselines assess the benefit of this architecture beyond supplying electronic information. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves magnetic anisotropy predictions, including for unseen ligands. It also improves excitation-energy predictions for dysprosium candidates with unseen ligands, extending the benefit to rotationally invariant scalar targets. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, it predicts real electron-spin correlations and low-field nuclear relaxation rates more accurately despite static crystal-field errors similar to the Hamiltonian-informed baseline. This dynamical advantage extends from water to methanol without retraining. These results support spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism in the tested systems and show why model selection should be guided by accuracy on the intended physical observables.

items.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
items.description: arXiv:2610.29196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.

items.title: Reconstruction differences rival individual differences in the fly compass connectome and break trained circuit models
items.description: arXiv:2610.29205v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural network models are increasingly constructed from synapse-resolution connectomes, and the same circuit is now available in reconstructions from other animals and pipelines. We do not know whether such models are dependent on the reconstruction they are built from, and whether connectome differences are biological or measurement errors. We studied the Drosophila head-direction circuit in nine versions: four flies (male CNS, hemibrain, FlyWire, BANC) and five variants of the same fly varying only by thresholds, proofreading or synapse detection. Using wiring-based correspondences validated by anatomical labels, we place all differences on one scale. A change of synapse detection within one fly changed the circuit more than halfway to the smallest between-fly difference on four distance measures; proofreading differences were smaller but depended on the metric, and left and right halves of one fly differed no more than random halves. Networks trained on each wiring to hold a cued heading developed near-perfect ring attractors, but their error increased from below 1 degree to 10-28 degrees when all weights changed by 1%. Training on each wiring did not transfer to any other connectome, including other versions of the same fly; refitting thirty cell-type gains, we repaired filtering-level differences but remaining error depended on wiring distance. Training with noise lowered precision and gave only partial transfer. In imaging data, the fly compass drifted gradually in darkness. Connectome-constrained models should report the reconstruction they were built on and be tested for robustness across reconstructions.

items.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage
items.description: arXiv:2610.30090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and unparseable. We present VX-One, a small multi-head network (100K--10M parameters) with calibrated typed outputs: a binary gate, a closed-set choice with an explicit unknown option where the benchmark supports it (and abstention elsewhere), and an ordinal score. Heads are temperature-calibrated, with 0.7--1.7 ms single-event CPU p50 latency. We evaluate UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, and EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP, and Kitsune baselines, and measure a Suricata-to-VX-One cascade over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Results are deliberately double-sided: on UNSW the gate ties the best baseline (0.9837+/-0.0002 versus MLP 0.9835+/-0.0013 across three seeds), while VX-One wins temporal CIC detection (0.734+/-0.022 versus 0.639+/-0.027) but loses multi-class attribution to XGBoost. Under leave-one-family-out, the gate detects all nine UNSW families but drops below chance on CIC recon; CIC trees transfer better. Suricata resolves only about 0.1% of attacks on flow reconstructions and 0.2--2.2% on payload-bearing PCAPs; the strictly by-day Phase 2 recovers only the in-scope DoS/DDoS share on the wave day (recall 0.34, precision 0.97). Calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partly survives. We contribute a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

items.title: "No human at the helm": Delaware plan would let AI agents run entire businesses
items.description: A Delaware proposal to let companies be operated by AI agents would help the firms' human owners evade legal responsibility for reckless and harmful actions taken by the AI, US Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) told Delaware Governor Matt Meyer in a letter yesterday. Comer, chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, told Meyer that the committee "seeks assistance obtaining documents related to your state administration’s efforts to establish a new form of corporate entity to be known as an Artificial Intelligence Company (AIC)." Comer said the proposal is ripe for abuse. "We are concerned that Delaware’s AIC proposal could be used to protect powerful AI companies and their investors from responsibility for reckless harmful actions, while also protecting non-transparent forces seeking anticompetitive regulatory capture behind state AI initiatives," Comer's letter said. items.title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
items.description: The Securities and Exchange Commission 's publication on Monday of Anthropic's S-1 form —ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company's quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI "rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down. Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic's S-1 "Risk Factors" section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally. After wading through Anthropic's book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we've narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look at what potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind. Read full article Comments

items.description: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge I'm at GitHub Universe this week and, similar to last year , the conference badge is a full-blown color screen computer. items.title: Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety” by Miles Brundage
items.description: This reading was previously included Day 2 of the BlueDot Governance course. In the newest version of the BlueDot Governance course, this reading is now optional. I was sad to see this reading removed because I think it’s a great provocation. However, since it’s no longer part of the core curriculum content, I’m publishing my notes separately from the rest of my day 2 notes. A short extract : Miles argues that: “At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)“: Pre-call content: At risk of taking you down a rabbit hole, I’ll add some context on this reading. Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. One of the most natural questions to ask is, “Why does Miles believe that we have so little time?” Fortunately, he links to a post that answers this question called Time’s Up for AI Policy (written Dec 2024). He writes: AI that exceeds human performance in nearly every cognitive domain is almost certain to be built and deployed in the next few years. The announcement of o3 today makes clear that superhuman coding and math are coming much sooner than many expected, and we have barely begun to think through or prepare for the implications of this This post links to a Tweet of his around the same time (we can also see his retrospective take from March this year): I’ll reshare some of my notes on maths progress here: OpenAI has reported solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem , which would be remarkably above trend if confirmed (there’s a dispute over whether someone else’s work made its way into the training data). However, it feels fair to say that the writing is on the wall (the mathematical community seems to agree, though there are a variety of perspectives on whether we’ll automate the components of a mathematicians job other than just producing proofs and how long that might take). They dropped 372 other results onto the internet and a few days ago, they dropped a few more results . Aside: Miles has a bet with Gary Marcus on AI progress. In July, Metaculus assigned Gary a 90% chance of winning, but more recently it dropped to 30%. I’ll share some additional alternate perspectives after the call, but for now I’ll share a quote from Richard Ngo: I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread I also have no doubt Eliezer Yudkowsky would be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing: When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get. .. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from. Post-call content: One reason why we might reject triage mode is if we broadly think AI progress is slower than folks at the labs think. We’ve already discussed this, but here’s two more considerations. Dwarkesh Patel has argued that timelines are longer than many folk expect because of a lack of continual learning and poor sample efficiency . Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL . He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling ). Towards the end of 2024, Steve Newman offered another possibility : what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we only become aware of the limitations of models over time?: “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.” “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.” Here’s a few other reasons why we might reject it: Toby Ord talks about broad AI

items.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
items.description: Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated , but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target. A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it's now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level. The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones. Read full article Comments
